column3: Direct continuation: Satan removes the garment and exposes shame, defining the threat to the protective layer.
Makes covering exposed shame a learned, concrete act, extending the focus's bodily covering function.
Shows clothing as honored adornment in security, though it adds little about the ethical garment.
Distinguishes taqwa's preventive protection from forgiveness after failure.
Sets the nearby moral boundary around public and hidden indecency, framing why concealment and taqwa matter.
Extends protection from the self to one's household against a grave consequence.
Names night itself as clothing, widening garment from body-cover to sheltering enclosure.
Offers a contrary enclosure: coverings become a punitive layer rather than protection.
Links lack of taqwa to repeated covenant-breaking, giving the inner garment an ethical test.
Shares rescue from an enemy but does not clarify garment, adornment, or taqwa.
Contrasts hiding from people with inescapable divine awareness, qualifying concealment.
No clear addition to the focus beyond a remote lexical association.
Does not materially clarify the focus's covering, adornment, or taqwa.

Too fragmentary to add a discernible reading of the focus.

A bare call to taqwa adds no distinct facet after earlier taqwa cards.
Straight path and remembrance are too general to clarify this verse.
The garden setting only weakly supports the adjacent clothing scene.

No clear relation to covering, adornment, or taqwa.

Absence of a protector is a general inverse parallel, not a close reading.

Connects worship to becoming muttaqin, but remains a general foundation.
Adam's lineage and responsive remembrance are too broad to add much.

Its relational restriction is only a broad limit-setting parallel.
Promise of gardens does not materially develop the focus.

Contrasts harmful mutual allegiance with God's guardianship of the muttaqin.
Trust and deliverance are relevant only at a broad ethical level.

The most muttaqi is kept away from fire, a direct but now redundant protection outcome.
Explicitly gives garments protection from heat and armor protection in conflict, closely joining clothing and safeguarding.
Returns to the first exposure: after the tree, the pair cover themselves with leaves from the garden.
Regulates displayed adornment and bodily covering, supplying a concrete social boundary for zina and concealment.
Outer garments are drawn close so persons are recognized and not harmed, an explicit protective use of dress.
Commands purification of garments, linking the outer layer with an ethical and ritual state.
Uses clothing as a contrary image for hunger and fear enveloping a community.
Treats outer-garment relaxation as bounded by non-display of adornment, refining the social clothing boundary.
Requires permission at three times of privacy, extending concealment to protected domestic intervals.
Bars entry into homes before permission and greeting, a complementary rule for guarded private space.
Restrains public display of adornment, a nearby counterpoint to permitted zina in 7:26 and 7:32.
Defines kinship exceptions around the screened household boundary, clarifying that boundaries have ordered scope.
Combines garden reward, adornment, and green garments, expanding the positive destination of lawful adornment.
Joins adornment with silk garments in the garden, supporting clothing as honored rather than merely concealing.
Repeats garden adornment and green silk garments, reinforcing the positive, rewarded aspect of dress.
Portrays green silk and brocade as garments of bliss, another positive counterpart to exposed shame.
The false blood-stained shirt makes a garment evidentiary, contrasting protective covering with deceptive appearance.
The torn shirt becomes physical evidence in a contested encounter, showing clothing can reveal rather than conceal.
The shirt's direction of tearing functions as discriminating evidence, qualifying any simple equation of covering with hiding.
Its back-side tearing distinguishes competing claims, a further instance of garment as exposed evidence.
The recognized shirt evidence turns appearance into moral accountability, a useful counter-reading of concealment.
A shirt mediates restoration of sight, a secondary positive extension of the garment motif.
Names wealth and children as worldly adornment, helping distinguish transient zina from enduring good deeds.
Catalogues beautified worldly desires, providing a cautionary boundary around adornment's attraction.
Associates adornment with a limited human mode of expression, a secondary check on reading rish as ultimate worth.
Frames worldly ornament as fleeting provision, complementing the focus's preference for the garment of taqwa.
Forbids excess in consuming provision, directly reinforcing the nearby command in 7:31.
Commands due giving and forbids waste, a parallel ethical limit on use of adornment and provision.
Identifies squanderers with satanic kinship, strengthening the local warning against excess beside the focus.
Praises spending between extravagance and stinginess, a balanced-use parallel to 7:31.
Permits good provision while forbidding transgression, another boundary for material gifts.
